subject: Soft-throttle proposal and true-up window for above-commit usage
messages:
From: Carlos Mendes <carlos@elliptic.ai>
To: jonas_weber@redwood.ai; marissa_cole@redwood.ai
Cc: procurement@elliptic.ai
Date: 2027-06-24T09:12:00Z
Subject: Re: Dedicated capacity — above-commit behavior and billing questions

Jonas / Marissa,

Thanks again for the demo last week — Elliptic AI is excited about moving from trial to a reserved GPU pool. Before we sign up for a 3-month commit, procurement needs clarity on two items we couldn't fully resolve:

1) If we exceed the committed pool (e.g., sustained spike for a 48-hour period), how does Redwood meter and bill that excess? Is it per-minute, per-hour, or per-token?
2) Do you provide any soft-throttle / priority routing rather than hard drops, and is there a grace or true-up window that avoids immediate high-rate charges?

Quick context: our traffic can spike 3-4x for short windows when new model rollouts happen. We're trying to understand operational risk and predictability for budgeting.

Attached: a short pricing table our finance team asked us to compare. Happy to hop on a call.

—Carlos
Head of Platform, Elliptic AI
From: jonas_weber@redwood.ai
To: Carlos Mendes <carlos@elliptic.ai>
Cc: marissa_cole@redwood.ai; aditya_rao@redwood.ai
Date: 2027-06-24T11:03:00Z
Subject: Re: Dedicated capacity — above-commit behavior and billing questions

Carlos — great questions. Short answer up front: we avoid black-box, per-token surprises and offer a tiered excess model with a short true-up window and a configurable soft-throttle policy. Below is the practical summary and a proposal for your SRE/finance review.

High-level approach
- Metering granularity: we meter on a 1-minute rolling window at the GPU-pool level (not per-request token accounting). This maps to capacity units (GPU-seconds) so it correlates with cost more directly than per-token billing for dedicated pools.
- Soft-throttle vs hard-throttle: default behavior is soft-throttle. When utilization exceeds commit for more than X minutes (configurable; proposal: 10 minutes sustained), we route new requests to a burst band with priority queuing. Requests remain in-flight; latency may increase but we avoid immediate drops.
- True-up & credits: we offer a 30-day true-up window where above-commit usage is aggregated and charged at a discounted overage tier (e.g., commit rate + 30%). For predictable spikes you can set a burst allowance (minutes per month) that is billed at a lower overage rate.

Proposal (what I'll put in the SOW/quote)
- Meter: 1-minute granularity, GPU-second accounting.
- Soft-throttle: grace threshold = 10 consecutive minutes over commit. When triggered: 80/20 priority split to committed vs burst queue; burst queue billed at overage rate.
- True-up: 30-day aggregation; invoices show committed, burst-minutes, and net true-up.
- Emergency hard-throttle: tenant opt-in for hard-throttle if you want firm limits.

I'll attach a matrix with numbers. Marissa — can you confirm standard overage tiers we should use for a 12 GPU equivalent pool for this customer (they indicated 12 x A100-eq in the call)? Aditya, can you include any operational constraints (concurrency caps, KV cache behavior) that matter for their rollout window?

If this sounds reasonable, we can convert it into a clause in the Dedicated SOW (true-up terms + burst allowance). Happy to sync live.

—Jonas
Director, Strategic Accounts
Redwood Inference
From: marissa_cole@redwood.ai
To: jonas_weber@redwood.ai; aditya_rao@redwood.ai
Date: 2027-06-24T12:05:00Z
Subject: Re: Dedicated capacity — above-commit behavior and billing questions

Jonas — copying the numbers I ran. For a 12-GPU committed pool (A100-eq), suggested overage tiers:
- Tier 1 (burst allowance): first 1,800 GPU-minutes/month (equivalent to 1 hour/day) at commit_rate * 1.15 (15% uplift).
- Tier 2 (sustained overage): next 10,800 GPU-minutes/month at commit_rate * 1.45 (45% uplift).
- Tier 3 (long-run overflow): any usage beyond that billed at on-demand-like rate commit_rate * 2.1.

Notes:
- The 1-minute granularity maps to our autoscaler and avoids per-request token noise.
- For their model rollouts we should recommend enabling prefix KV caching to reduce burst token compute; that reduces effective burst minutes by ~20% in our simulations.
- For the SOW I'll include an optional 90-day ramp credit where we discount Tier 1 by 50% for the first 90 days if they sign a 12-month commitment.

Attaching the pricing matrix and a one-page true-up flow that finance can reference.

—Marissa
Senior Solutions Engineer
Redwood Inference
Attachment stubs: dedicated_pricing_matrix_v2.xlsx (xlsx), proposed-trueup-sla.pdf (pdf)
From: Carlos Mendes <carlos@elliptic.ai>
To: jonas_weber@redwood.ai; marissa_cole@redwood.ai
Cc: procurement@elliptic.ai
Date: 2027-06-25T07:18:00Z
Subject: Re: Dedicated capacity — above-commit behavior and billing questions

Thanks, this is very helpful. A few follow-ups from procurement and our SRE lead:

- Procurement: can you make the Tier 1 burst allowance explicit in the SOW and show sample invoices (committed / Tier1 / Tier2) so we can model cashflow?
- SRE: what happens to in-flight requests when soft-throttle engages — do you queue indefinitely or reject after N seconds? We need a default rejection (TTL) behavior to surface to our app teams.

Also, about the 30-day true-up: is that a single invoice line item at month-end or do you show daily metering details? We prefer daily metering CSVs for internal chargeback.

If we can get those two clarifications, procurement is ready to push a PO.

—Carlos
From: aditya_rao@redwood.ai
To: Carlos Mendes <carlos@elliptic.ai>; jonas_weber@redwood.ai; marissa_cole@redwood.ai
Date: 2027-06-25T15:47:00Z
Subject: Re: Dedicated capacity — above-commit behavior and billing questions

Carlos — quick answers from the runtime team: 

- In-flight behavior: soft-throttle uses a priority queue with a configurable request TTL. Default policy: queue up to 45s; if not scheduled by then we return a 503 + Retry-After header. For streamed responses we continue to stream while the request is accepted. We can reduce TTL to 10s if you prefer lower latency guarantees.
- Metering detail: we publish daily meter CSVs at the tenant level (per-minute aggregates) with columns {timestamp, gpu_minutes, queue_length_avg, burst_flag}. The month-end invoice line shows consolidated committed vs burst vs long-run overflow, but you get the CSVs for chargeback and auditing.
- Implementation note: enabling KV prefix caching and a small local request cache for repeated prompts reduces observed burst load. We can toggle that in the deployment and include a configuration section in the SOW.

I'll update the SOW draft with: explicit Tier1 allowance, sample invoice lines, daily meter CSV link, and TTL default. Will circulate for signature once Jonas approves.

—Aditya
Senior Product Manager, Runtime
Redwood Inference
